input: Client went silent for 10 days after I sent the proposal. Need to follow up without sounding desperate.
reply: Hi, I hope you are doing well. I wanted to check in on the proposal I sent last week — no rush at all, I just wanted to make sure it reached you. If you have any questions, or if the timing has changed, I am happy to adjust.
explanation: Hedged follow-up with a face-saving excuse (maybe it did not arrive) avoids sounding pushy.

input: Long-term client asks me to do weekend work regularly. I want to keep weekends free.
reply: Hi! I love working with you, and I want to keep doing great work together — which is why I keep weekends free to recharge. I am always available during the week, and for genuine rush jobs we can agree a rush rate. Does that sound fair?
explanation: Frames the boundary as protecting the quality of the shared work, with a rush-rate option.

input: Sent a quote 2 days ago, no reply yet. Light second touch.
reply: Hi, just checking in — did you get a chance to look at the quote? Happy to answer any questions.
explanation: Short, direct, low-imposition check-in.

input: Long-term client wants one more tiny revision after the limit, I will do it free but note the limit.
reply: Hi! Of course, I will squeeze in this last little tweak for you — no charge this time. Just a gentle note that we are past the included rounds now, so the next set of changes I will need to quote. Thanks for understanding!
explanation: A free favour framed with warmth, plus a soft note that the limit now applies.

input: Client asked for a full extra section after we signed off the design. Need to charge for it.
reply: Hello, thanks for the new section idea. Since it falls outside the signed-off design, I would need to quote it separately — I can send a short estimate today. Would you like me to go ahead with that?
explanation: Polite, formal framing of extra work as a separate quote, with a question that leaves the decision to the client.

input: Long-term client is unhappy with one deliverable and asks for a partial refund. I want to offer a fix first.
reply: Hi, I am really sorry that piece missed the mark — I value our work together and I want to make it right. Before we talk about a refund, could I take one more pass at it? If it still does not work for you, we will sort out a partial refund together.
explanation: Relationship-first: apology, a fix attempt, and a conditional refund promise.

input: Client overpaid by $50 by mistake and asks for it back. Easy yes.
reply: Hi, thanks for flagging it — you are right, there is an extra $50. I have sent it back just now. Let me know once you see it!
explanation: A clear mistake, small amount: direct acknowledgement and action is the polite response.

input: Long-term client is shouting in the call and being disrespectful. Need to set a boundary calmly.
reply: I hear that you are frustrated, and I want to sort this out. I would ask that we keep the conversation respectful so we can fix the issue together. Could we take a short break and come back to the specific points?
explanation: Names the behaviour without accusing, requests respect, and proposes a pause — a firm boundary in hedged language.

input: Client demands a full refund after I delivered the work and they used it, claiming they are not satisfied.
reply: Hello, I am sorry to hear the work did not meet your expectations. The files were delivered as agreed and have been in use, so a full refund would not be possible. I would be glad to revise the specific parts you are unhappy with, or we could discuss a partial credit toward future work.
explanation: Apology plus a factual statement and two alternatives, instead of a flat no.

input: Client disagrees with my revision policy and says other freelancers do unlimited revisions.
reply: Hi, I completely understand — different freelancers work differently, and I appreciate you raising it. My revision limit is there so I can give each round proper attention rather than rushing. I am happy to discuss a package with more rounds included if that would help.
explanation: Positive politeness validates the client's view, explains the policy's purpose, and offers an alternative.

input: Client asks to lower my hourly rate from $40 to $25 because the project is long.
reply: Hi, I appreciate you raising this. My rate is $40, and I am not able to lower it further, but for a longer project I am happy to adjust the scope so the total fits your budget. Would you like to go through the scope together?
explanation: Firm on rate, flexible on scope — a classic hedged negotiation that protects the freelancer's price.

input: New client offers $50 for a website that normally costs $500. Need to decline politely and state my rate.
reply: Hello, thank you for reaching out and for thinking of me. I am afraid $50 would not cover the work involved in a full website. My rate for this kind of project starts at $400 — I would be happy to adjust the scope to fit a smaller budget if that helps.
explanation: Thanks, hedged refusal, clear rate, and a scope-adjustment offer keep the door open.

input: Long-term client is usually on time but this invoice is 5 days late. Gentle nudge needed.
reply: Hi there! Just a friendly nudge on the latest invoice — it looks like it slipped past its due date by a few days. Whenever you get a moment, could you take a look? Thanks so much, as always, for being great to work with.
explanation: Positive politeness (warmth, shared history) fits a long-term relationship and a low-stakes delay.

input: Client wants a 7th revision and a full redesign of the logo, still within the original fixed price.
reply: Hi, I would be glad to explore a new direction for the logo. Since we are beyond the included revision rounds, I would need to treat a redesign as a separate piece of work. Shall I send a short estimate for it so you can decide?
explanation: Hedged framing plus a question keeps the boundary polite while offering a priced way forward.

input: I over-promised and cannot deliver on time. Need to own it and ask for 5 more days.
reply: Hi, I want to be upfront: I will not be able to deliver by Friday as planned, and I take responsibility for that. Would it be possible to have until next Wednesday? I am working on it daily and will send you a progress update on Monday so you are not left waiting.
explanation: Owning the delay plus hedging and a concrete update plan preserves trust while asking for a big extension.

input: Client thanked me warmly and asked if I am available next month. Confirm and keep the relationship warm.
reply: Hi, thank you — working with you has been a real pleasure! Yes, I am available next month and I would love to work together again. Just send the details whenever you are ready.
explanation: Warm reciprocation and an easy yes keep a good relationship warm.

input: Client has not paid invoice #1048, now 12 days overdue. I need the money but do not want to sound rude.
reply: Hi, I hope your week is going well. I wanted to follow up on invoice #1048, which was due 12 days ago. Could you let me know when I can expect the payment? Happy to resend the invoice if that helps.
explanation: Hedged request plus an offer of help reduces the imposition while keeping the deadline clear.

input: Client asked for the invoice to be resent because they lost the original. Payment is a week late.
reply: Hi, no problem at all — I have attached the invoice again for your convenience. Could you let me know once the payment is on its way? I appreciate it.
explanation: Minimising the inconvenience (no problem at all) and a short hedged request keep a small delay low-conflict.

input: Client keeps adding extra pages and features that were not in the agreed scope, without extra pay.
reply: Hi, thanks for sharing these additions. They go a little beyond what we agreed in the original scope, so I would like to treat them as a separate task with its own estimate. Could we agree on that before I start, so the main delivery stays on track?
explanation: Hedged boundary-setting: acknowledges the request, names the scope issue, and proposes a separate paid task.

input: Need to shift a 30-minute call by one hour tomorrow.
reply: Hi, could we move our call tomorrow from 10:00 to 11:00? Thanks!
explanation: Tiny, low-imposition ask — a direct question is enough.

input: Client read my message but did not reply for a week. Follow up with a clear next step and deadline.
reply: Hi, following up on my last message. Could you let me know by Friday whether you would like to go ahead? If the timing no longer works, no problem at all — I just need to free up the slot.
explanation: Gives the client an easy out (timing changed) while setting a clear decision date.

input: The client added three new pages mid-project and still expects the original deadline. I need an extra week.
reply: Hello, thank you for sharing the additional pages. With the extra scope, delivering everything to the same standard by the original date would be difficult. Would it be possible to extend the deadline by one week? I am happy to prioritise the most urgent pages first if that helps.
explanation: Hedging, a clear reason, and an offer to prioritise make a large ask acceptable to a new client.

input: Client said the design is wrong without saying what is wrong. Need specifics without sounding defensive.
reply: Hi, thanks for the feedback. I wonder if you could walk me through which parts feel off to you — it would help me get the next version much closer to what you have in mind.
explanation: An indirect hint (I wonder if) asks for specifics without directly challenging the vague criticism.

input: Client asks me to share another client's confidential work as a reference. Must refuse.
reply: Hi, I am afraid I cannot share another client's work — I keep every client's material confidential, just as I would yours. I am happy to share anonymised samples of my own work instead, or we can discuss what you need and I will create a fresh example.
explanation: Refusal grounded in a principle that also protects this client, plus an alternative.

input: Client is on revision round 6, contract allows 2. Need to say further revisions are chargeable.
reply: Hi, thanks for all the detailed feedback — we have now used the two revision rounds included in the project. I am happy to keep refining, and further rounds would be charged at my usual hourly rate. Would you like me to send a quick estimate for the next round?
explanation: Acknowledges the client's input, states the contract fact, and offers a priced next step.

input: Client messages me at midnight and expects instant replies. Need to set working hours.
reply: Hi, thanks for the message. Just a quick note on my working hours: I reply between 9am and 6pm on weekdays, so anything sent in the evening I will pick up first thing in the morning. For anything truly urgent, please mark it urgent and I will do my best.
explanation: States the boundary as information, not a complaint, with an urgent-message exception.

input: I need two more days on the homepage redesign to keep the quality high, deadline is Friday.
reply: Hi, I wanted to check in on the homepage redesign. To keep the quality as high as possible, would it be possible to move the deadline to Monday? I am on track with the rest of the work and will share a progress update on Friday either way.
explanation: Hedged request with a reason (quality) and a reassurance about progress reduces the imposition.

input: Client wants me to also manage their social media, which was never discussed. Need to decline or price it.
reply: Hello, thanks for thinking of me for the social media work. That sits outside the current project, but I would be happy to look at it as a separate monthly service. Would you like a short proposal and price for that?
explanation: Thanks plus hedging turns a scope expansion into an optional separate service instead of a refusal.

input: Client asked for a tiny text change that is technically out of scope but takes 2 minutes.
reply: Hi, sure — I have made that small text change for you. Let me know if you spot anything else.
explanation: Trivial effort, low imposition: a direct yes is the polite move.

input: Client's budget is half my rate but the project is interesting and short. Offer a reduced scope.
reply: Hi, thanks for sharing your budget. My full rate for this would be $400, but I could deliver a smaller version — the core pages without the extra animations — for $200. Would that work for you?
explanation: States the rate clearly, then proposes a concrete smaller scope that fits the budget.

input: Client wants daily progress calls, I prefer a weekly update. Suggest a lighter rhythm.
reply: Hi, could we switch to one weekly progress update instead of daily calls? I will send a short written update every Friday, and you can reach me anytime by email in between.
explanation: Low-stakes process change: a direct proposal with a concrete alternative.

input: New client said the first draft is excellent and asked what else I can do for them.
reply: Hi, thank you — I am glad you like it! I can also help with the social media graphics and the landing page copy if that would be useful. Shall I send a short note on both?
explanation: A compliment is a natural opening for a direct, low-pressure upsell.

input: Long-term client disappeared mid-project for 2 weeks. I need to know if the project is still on.
reply: Hi, I hope everything is alright on your side. I have not heard from you in a couple of weeks, so I wanted to check whether the project is still going ahead. If you need a pause, that is completely fine — I just need to plan my schedule. Let me know either way?
explanation: Concern for the client plus a low-pressure request for a yes/no answer.

input: Startup with a tiny budget asks for a logo. I can do a simple version cheaply.
reply: Hi, thanks for reaching out! For a simple one-page logo I can do $80. Let me know if that works for you.
explanation: Low-stakes, clear offer: direct pricing is appropriate.

input: Invoice due tomorrow, want to send a polite reminder in advance so it does not slip.
reply: Hi, just a quick heads-up that invoice #1048 is due tomorrow. Thanks so much!
explanation: Low imposition and a routine reminder need no hedging; a direct short note is appropriate.

input: Client said my work is terrible and demanded a redo in an aggressive tone.
reply: Hi, I am sorry the work did not meet your expectations — that is the last thing I want. Could you tell me specifically what did not work, so I can address it properly? I want to make sure the next version is right.
explanation: Apology and a request for specifics de-escalate without accepting the insult or the blame.

input: Client loves the work but wants me to commit to a big new project at the old rate. Need to renegotiate.
reply: Hello, thank you for the trust — I am glad the work landed well. For a project of this size, my rate would be $50 an hour rather than the $40 from the first project, given the scope and the timeline. I am happy to walk through the estimate with you.
explanation: Hedged rate rise for a bigger commitment, with an offer to explain the estimate.

input: Client paid a deposit, then cancelled before I started. Contract says deposit is non-refundable, need to explain.
reply: Hello, thank you for letting me know. As noted in our agreement, the deposit reserves the time slot and is non-refundable once the project is booked. I am happy to keep the deposit as credit for a future project within the next three months if that helps.
explanation: Cites the agreement neutrally and offers credit, softening a refusal to refund.

input: Long-term client loves my work and wants to extend the contract. Negotiate a slightly higher rate for the extension.
reply: Hi, thank you — I have loved our work together and I would be delighted to continue. For the extension, my rate has moved to $45 an hour to reflect the scope we have grown into. I think the results speak for themselves, and I would love to keep delivering them for you.
explanation: Gratitude and shared history soften a rate rise, tied to the value already delivered.

input: Client threatened a bad review unless I work for free this weekend.
reply: Hi, I am sorry you are unhappy with the timeline. I am afraid I cannot take on unpaid weekend work, but I am happy to look at what can be done within the current schedule. If you would like, we can discuss a small paid rush option.
explanation: Refuses the threat calmly, does not mention the review, and offers a priced alternative.
